newsitem.title: SPAIN: Picasso's Guernica stirs emotions in Spain - again.
newsitem.headline: Picasso's Guernica stirs emotions in Spain - again.

text.p: Basques reacted with outrage on Wednesday to a Madrid art gallery's refusal to loan Pablo Picasso's anti-war masterpiece "Guernica" to their new Guggenheim Museum.

Officials at the Reina Sofia contemporary art museum said the vast painting, measuring almost 12 feet by 26 (3.6 by 7.8 metres), had suffered too much damage in previous moves to risk another transfer and denied the Guggenheim request.
The Guggenheim Museum, backed by the Basque regional government, had hoped to use Guernica as the centrepiece of its inauguration on October 3 in Bilbao.

Sixty years after it was painted to illustrate the 1937 Nazi bombardment of the Basque nationalist shrine Guernica, Picasso's controversial work has once again showed an uncanny ability to provoke strong reactions among Spaniards.

"As always, the bombs are in Euskadi (the Basque region) and the art is in Madrid, which has handled this affair with very little tact," Basque Nationalist Party leader Xabier Arzalluz told journalists on Wednesday.
"It's inexcusable that the Guernica has been shown in 32 cities in the world and it is precisely when there's a request for its transfer to Euskadi that it can't be transferred."

Basques have campaigned in the past for the painting, which they say belongs in the town of Guernica, venerated as the cradle of the Basque people. The region is home to a strong separatist movement calling for an independent Basque state encompassing parts of northern Spain and southern France.
In 1987, Basque radicals stormed the Prado Museum where it was then held to demand its transfer.

Picasso painted the black, grey and white work for the 1937 World Fair in Paris as testament to the suffering of the Spanish Civil War. Some 2,000 people died in the first mass bombing of civilians by German allies of General Francisco Franco.
A lifelong opponent of dictator Franco, the artist vowed the painting would not enter Spain until democracy was restored. He died in 1973 and never saw his dream realised.

The painting was shown in exile as a symbol of the horrors of war and finally, after much controversy, brought to Spain in 1981. Ten years later, again amid protests, it was transferred to the Reina Sofia -- hoped to be its final home.

Reina Sofia officials said politics played no part in the transfer denial, which was based on an exhaustive technical analysis of the canvas. They said the painting was simply too big and had been moved too many times before to be moved again.
Museum authorities said they had turned down requests by Paris, Japan and Barcelona for the same reason.

"The Guernica is enormously valuable in the history of contemporary art and its physical state must be looked after," Valeriano Bozal, president of the museum's patrons, said on Tuesday. "It should not be moved to another museum."
But Bilbao Guggenhemim president Josu Bergara said the parent museum in New York had a technical report saying the painting could be moved with little risk of damage.

Basque officials said the central government was afraid of losing control of the painting, which is an important symbol of democracy for all Spaniards and the star attraction of the Reina Sofia's otherwise lacklustre collection.
"It's disenchanting and frustrating," Bergara said in a statement. "The decision is a grave error...culturally and politically."
